blocks.text: **The problem.** Build a queue on a singly linked list of `ListNode`s (each has a `val` and a `next`). Support `enqueue(x)`, `dequeue()` (remove and return the front item, or **-1** if empty), `front()` (the front item, or **-1** if empty), `isEmpty()` and `size()`. A linked list never runs out of slots, so there is no capacity to manage.

blocks.alt: A linked list 10, 20, 30 used as a queue. The head node, 10, is the front, where items are dequeued. The tail node, 30, is the back, where items are enqueued.

blocks.code:
enqueue(10)   enqueue(20)   front()   -> 10
dequeue()     -> 10         size()    -> 1
dequeue()     -> 20         dequeue() -> -1  (empty)

blocks.text: A linked list can only cheaply change things it holds a pointer to. So the questions are: **which end is the front, which is the back, and which pointers do we keep?**
1. Brute force: only a head pointer

Dequeue at the **head**: point `head` at the second node and the first falls away — O(1). But enqueue has to add after the **last** node, and with only `head` we must walk the whole list to find it every time.

blocks.alt: Enqueue 40 with only a head pointer. The list is 10, 20, 30. To attach 40 after 30, the code walks from the head: step 1 at 10, step 2 at 20, step 3 at 30, the last node. Every enqueue repeats this O(n) walk.

elements.text: enqueue 40: walk from head to the last node first, O(n)
elements.originalText: enqueue 40: walk from head to the last node first, O(n)

blocks.text: **enqueue O(n); dequeue, front, isEmpty and size O(1); space O(n).**
2. Optimal: keep a tail pointer too
Remember the last node in a second pointer, `tail`. Enqueue links the new node after `tail` and moves `tail` to it — no walk. Dequeue still happens at `head`.

blocks.alt: Enqueue 40 with a tail pointer. The old tail, 30, gets a next arrow to the new node 40, and tail moves to 40. Head stays on 10. Nothing is walked: O(1).

elements.text: enqueue 40: tail.next = node, then tail = node, O(1)
elements.originalText: enqueue 40: tail.next = node, then tail = node, O(1)

blocks.text: Why not the other way round — enqueue at the head, dequeue at the tail? Removing the **last** node means making the node **before** it the new tail, and a singly linked list can't step backwards. Finding that node is an O(n) walk, even with a tail pointer. So: **dequeue at the head, enqueue at the tail.**

blocks.alt: The list 10, 20, 30 with tail on 30. To remove 30, the code would need the node before it, 20, but a singly linked list has no arrow pointing backwards.

elements.text: no arrow points backwards: finding 20 is an O(n) walk
elements.originalText: no arrow points backwards: finding 20 is an O(n) walk

blocks.text: One trap: when the **last** node is dequeued, `head` becomes null — and `tail` must be set to null **as well**. Forget it, and `tail` still points at the removed node; the next enqueue links the new item onto a node that is no longer in the queue, and it's lost.

blocks.caption: Try the "Empty again" example: the queue empties, and both pointers must reset.

blocks.text: **Every operation O(1); space O(n)** — one node per item, and the queue never needs to grow or copy.
3. Best solution: a circular list with one pointer

Two pointers work, but there's a neater trick that needs only **one**. Make the list **circular**: the last node's `next` points back to the first. Now keep just `tail`. The front is always `tail.next`, one step away, so both ends are still reachable in O(1) — and there's only one pointer to keep correct.

blocks.alt: A circular list 10, 20, 30. 30 is the tail, and its next arrow curves back to 10, the front. The only pointer kept is tail; the front is tail.next.

elements.text: the back points round to the front
elements.originalText: the back points round to the front

blocks.text: **Enqueue** puts the new node between `tail` and the front, then makes it the tail. **Dequeue** removes `tail.next` by pointing `tail.next` one node further on. A queue with **one** node points at itself — and dequeueing that last node sets `tail` to null.

**Every operation O(1); space O(n)** with a single pointer. It's no faster than the two-pointer version — the gain is one less field to keep in sync, which is why this is a favourite interview follow-up.

rows.approach: Brute force: only a head pointer
rows.timeWhy: Each `enqueue` **walks the whole list** to find the last node; dequeue is O(1).
rows.spaceWhy: One node per item, and **one pointer**.

rows.approach: Optimal: keep a tail pointer too
rows.timeWhy: Enqueue at the **tail**, dequeue at the **head**: no walking.
rows.spaceWhy: One node per item, plus **two pointers**.

rows.approach: Best: a circular list with one pointer
rows.timeWhy: The front is always `tail.next`, so **one pointer** reaches both ends.
rows.spaceWhy: One node per item, and **a single pointer**.

blocks.text: **Array or linked list underneath?** Both give O(1) operations. The circular array from the last problem is usually faster in practice: its items sit side by side in memory, which the CPU cache loves, and it doesn't allocate a node per item. The linked list never copies anything and never wastes spare slots. Java's `ArrayDeque` (an array) usually beats its `LinkedList` for exactly this reason.

items: **dequeue and front on an empty queue** — return -1 without touching a null pointer.
**Empty, then used again** — enqueue 5, dequeue, enqueue 6, front: must give 6. This catches a `tail` that wasn't reset.
**A single item** — in the circular version, one node points at itself; dequeueing it must set `tail` to null.
**Long runs** — many enqueues, then many dequeues: the order must stay first in, first out.
**Deque on a doubly linked list** — add `prev` pointers and both ends can add **and** remove in O(1).
**LRU cache** — a doubly linked list used as a queue (least recently used at the front), plus a hash map to jump to any node.
**Queue using two stacks** — later in this course: a queue built from a completely different structure.
**Queue on an array** — the previous problem: a circular buffer instead of nodes.
